children: 0953 GMT - U.S. Treasury yields and the dollar decline due to falling oil prices, a retreat in market expectations of a Federal Reserve rate hike in September and a stronger yen. New York Fed President John Williams told CNBC Wednesday that he saw no clear signs of a necessity to raise interest rates for now. That said, the possibility of a Fed rate hike this month could "continue to underpin Treasury yields and limit the dollar's downside," Sky Links Capital Group's Daniel Takieddine says in a note. The DXY dollar index falls 0.4% to a six-day low of 99.166. The 10-year U.S. Treasury yield falls 1.8 basis points to 4.774%, having reached a near three-year high of 4.818% on Wednesday, according to Tradeweb data. (emese.bartha@wsj.com)

0932 GMT - The U.A.E.'s non-oil private sector expanded at its strongest pace since December 2024 in August, with the S&P Global Purchasing Managers' Index rising to 55.3 from 52.7 in July. New business and output growth accelerated sharply as activity recovered from earlier conflict-related disruption. Dubai's PMI also strengthened, rising to 54.1 from 51.7. The readings point to renewed momentum in the U.A.E.'s non-oil economy after the slowdown earlier in the summer, S&P Global says. (farhan.rafid@wsj.com)

0905 GMT - Saudi Arabia's non-oil private sector gains momentum in August, with the Riyad Bank Saudi Arabia Purchasing Managers' Index rising to 53.8 from 53.1 in July, its highest level in six months, S&P Global says. Output growth accelerated and hiring strengthened as domestic demand remained resilient, while supply conditions improved. Export demand remained comparatively weak, however, indicating that the expansion continues to be driven largely by domestic activity. (farhan.rafid@wsj.com)

0859 GMT - Overseas investors pricing in a more hawkish BOJ and adjustments in portfolio positioning by real-money investors at the beginning of the month are sending the yen higher, State Street strategist Masahiko Loo says in a note. The yen hit its strongest intraday levels since Aug. 3, with the dollar last down 1.3% at 156.62 yen. While the carry trade still works, "it is no longer a free lunch," the strategist says. "Markets are finally starting to buy into the idea that Japan may continue normalizing policy into 2027," he says. Traders are becoming less comfortable running aggressive short-yen positions as they more cautiously assess a more hawkish BOJ path, Loo notes. (sherry.qin@wsj.com)

0840 GMT - A possible interest-rate rise by the U.S. Federal Reserve in September could cause the yen to fall versus the dollar, ING's Chris Turner says in a note. The yen jumps against the dollar on Thursday amid chatter of potential intervention. For yen gains to continue, however, this could require an increased pace of interest-rate hikes by the Bank of Japan, Turner says. "Any sustainable turn lower in dollar/yen now probably requires a much more hawkish Bank of Japan and some new initiatives to encourage domestic investment in Japan." The dollar falls 1.0% to 157.14 yen, having hit a one month-low of 156.34 yen earlier, LSEG data show. Markets price a 59% chance of a Fed rate increase in September.(miriam.mukuru@wsj.com)

0828 GMT - The dollar falls to its lowest in nearly a week against a basket of currencies, helped by sharp gains in the Japanese yen amid chatter of potential intervention to prop it up after recent declines. The DXY dollar index falls to a six-day low of 99.166 as the U.S. currency drops more than 1% to a one-month low of 156.34 yen, LSEG data show. The yen's sharp jump has had "a knock-on negative impact on the dollar," ING's Francesco Pesole says in a note. Also weighing on the dollar are Wednesday's weak U.S. ADP private payrolls data and comments from New York Fed President John Williams that there is no clear evidence for now to suggest interest rates need to rise. (jessica.fleetham@wsj.com)

0751 GMT - The Debt Management Office sale of 900 million pounds ($1.2 billion) in the September 2049 index-linked gilt due at 0900 GMT is expected to attract demand given the gilt's strong performance over the past year, RBC Capital Markets strategists say in a note. "The price action is clearly indicative of strong demand for the bond/sector and hence we expect the auction to go fine." In addition, index-linked gilts look more attractive than nominal gilts, given slow U.K. economic growth and elevated energy costs which helped lift 10-year and 30-year nominal gilt yields to multiyear highs this week, they say. (miriam.mukuru@wsj.com)

0749 GMT - Gold prices rise more than 1% as the ​dollar weakened after U.S. private payrolls data pointed to slower job growth in August. Investors are now focused on interest-rate expectations, oil prices and bond yields worldwide. "While the market is pricing a more than 60% probability of a September rate hike, the question remains whether the Fed will tighten that close to the November midterm elections," analysts at Saxo Bank say. "For now, gold's inverse correlation with oil prices and bond yields remains a key focus, sidelining other potentially supportive drivers," they say. In early European trading, futures are up 1.3% at $4,472.20 a troy ounce. (giulia.petroni@wsj.com)

0720 GMT - Yields on U.K. government bonds, or gilts, decline, tracking their U.S. equivalents and helped by lower oil prices. This comes after developed-market sovereign bond yields climbed to multiyear highs in recent sessions, mainly driven by inflation concerns. Ten-year gilt yields hit a 19-year high of 5.294% on Wednesday, while 10-year Bund yields hit their highest since 2011, LSEG data show. Market focus is on U.S. non-farm payrolls data due to be released on Friday. Ten-year gilt yields fall 4.1 basis points to last trade at 5.198%. (miriam.mukuru@wsj.com)

0720 GMT - Australia's 2Q GDP data this week highlighted the problem at the core of the economy. Productivity in remains alarmingly low, says Tapas Strickland, economist at Moomoo Australia. Labor productivity, measured as GDP per hour worked, was flat in the quarter, remaining at the same level it was in 2019. There has been no productivity growth for almost seven years, he adds. This is why anaemic economic growth is still leading to inflation, with markets pricing in a greater chance of a September RBA, Strickland says. (james.glynn@wsj.com; X @JamesGlynnWSJ)

0711 GMT - Bitcoin rises modestly as investors look to diversify their investments amid high global market uncertainty. Investors await monthly U.S. jobs data due on Friday to gain clues on the possible path of U.S. Federal Reserve rate decisions. This follows weaker-than-expected U.S. ADP private payrolls data on Wednesday. Weaker data could push yields and the dollar lower, supporting bitcoin "if markets interpret the data as controlled cooling rather than a severe growth shock," says Mariia Menahem, CEO of Clarity Global, in a note. Bitcoin rises 0.5% to $77,784. (miriam.mukuru@wsj.com)

0709 GMT - Japan's PM Sanae Takaichi is unlikely to change her loose fiscal policy stance unless the 10-year JGB yield rises rapidly above 3.5% and stays there, SMBC Nikko Securities economists say. Under her growth strategy centered on massive domestic investments, real GDP growth is projected to accelerate to 1.1% in FY 2030 and 1.8% in FY 2040, they say. That would help the national and local debt-to-GDP ratio decline steadily, they add. If the 10-year JGB yield remains around 3% and the investment program is successful, the government can hit its debt-reduction targets, making policy changes unlikely at this level, the economists note. The 10-year JGB yield was last at 2.965%.(megumi.fujikawa@wsj.com)
